extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (authors of research papers), especially combinatorics researchers and graduate students writing papers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on how to open a mathematics research paper (especially in combinatorics): when to 'get to the point' vs when to prepare the reader, and how to write a short Foreword/opening that explains the philosophy or high‑level idea before stating main results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Get-to-the-point opening (when appropriate)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Starting a paper is easy. That is, if you don’t care for the marketing, don’t want to be memorable, and just want to get on with the story and quickly communicate what you have proved."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach works when the story is very simple (e.g., 'here is a famous conjecture which we solve in this paper') because the background/context has been told elsewhere. It's an efficient direct opening but assumes readers already know the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare the reader for complicated stories
rubrics_metrics.description: "If your story is more complicated, this 'get to the point' approach doesn’t really work... Essentially you need to prepare the reader for what’s to come."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For complex narratives or layered results, invest in exposition up front so readers can follow the later technical statements and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write a Foreword before the main result
rubrics_metrics.description: "I recommend writing the Foreword — a paragraph or two devoted to philosophy underlying your work or a high level explanation of the key idea in your paper before you proceed to state the main result."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place this short Foreword ahead of formal theorem statements to give readers the conceptual roadmap. It should be high-level and philosophical or explanatory rather than technical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreword: include memorable/literary description
rubrics_metrics.description: "Consider putting in the Foreword some highly literary description of what you are doing. If it’s beautiful or sufficiently memorable, it might be quoted in other papers... and bring some extra clicks to your work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A striking, well‑phrased opening can increase the paper's visibility and make ideas easier to recall. This is optional marketing as well as exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreword content suggestions (big picture, motivations, principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Feel free to discuss the big picture, NSF project outline style, mention some motivational examples in other fields of study, general physical or philosophical principles underlying your work, etc."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Foreword to situate the problem: explain motivations, cross‑disciplinary connections, conceptual principles, or illustrative examples that make the contribution meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreword length guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: "I doubt referees would object if you keep your Foreword under one page."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the Foreword concise — a paragraph or two, and definitely short (roughly under a page) so it complements rather than distracts from the main results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid starting with dry technical definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice from Martin Krieger: "Don’t Just Begin with 'Let A be an algebra…'" (i.e., avoid beginning with sterile technical set‑up).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opening immediately with definitions and symbols is often unmemorable and alienating; prefer an opening that gives intuition or a conceptual frame before formalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use opening lines that can appeal beyond specialists
rubrics_metrics.description: The author gathered varied opening lines that are "less closely related to the subject matter of the article, so might appeal to broader audience."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft openings that can engage non‑specialists or readers from adjacent areas when appropriate — this can broaden impact and make the paper more readable.

rubrics_metrics.name: When judging combinatorics results: naturalness and elegance matter
rubrics_metrics.description: "Judging the importance of the results is also relatively easy: the more natural or interesting the objects are, and the stronger or more elegant is the final formula, the better."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In enumerative combinatorics specifically, emphasize natural/interesting objects and elegant/strong formulas in the exposition and opening to convey significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context can be superfluous for some combinatorics results
rubrics_metrics.description: "In fact, the story or the context behind the results is usually superfluous since they speak for themselves."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For some simple counting results, a brief direct statement may suffice; but be mindful of when extra context is needed (see the 'prepare the reader' criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: When attacking large open problems, start with natural special cases
rubrics_metrics.description: "How do you approach a massive open problem with countless cases to consider? You start from the beginning... trying to resolve either the most natural, the most interesting or the simplest yet out of reach special cases."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the opening, explain which special cases you tackle and why (most natural/interesting/simplest) to show scope and strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: State whether a technical inequality/result is a tool or an object of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: "There are two schools of thought on what to do when an interesting combinatorial inequality is established... treat it as a tool... or treat the inequality as a result of importance in its own right."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify in the introduction whether a technical lemma/inequality is mainly a tool toward applications or the central object; this guides exposition and subsequent emphasis on proof style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek 'right proofs' and multiple proofs when illuminating
rubrics_metrics.description: "When it comes to fundamental results, one proof is rarely enough, and one is often on the prowl for a better, more elegant or more direct proof... different proofs elucidate different aspects..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the opening/foreword, mention if multiple proofs exist or are sought and how they contribute differently to understanding; this frames readers' expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value combinatorial interpretations and direct bijections
rubrics_metrics.description: "Finding a combinatorial interpretation is an everlasting problem... A direct bijection is the most natural approach... restores order..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your work provides combinatorial interpretations or bijections, highlight them early as they give conceptual insight and connect to broader themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the broader significance or 'miracle' and place it in a scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: "There is more than one way to explain a miracle... investigate away every consequence and implication... place the apparent miracle as a part of the general scheme."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a surprising result appears, use the Foreword/introduction to show consequences, implications, or how it fits into a larger pattern — this demystifies and increases impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and applications to judge and communicate theory
rubrics_metrics.description: "A combinatorial theory is often judged not by its intrinsic beauty but by the examples and applications... While eternally challenging, this helps to keep the area lively, widely accessible, and growing..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the opening, include representative examples/applications where appropriate to demonstrate usefulness and relevance.
